person.name: Bryle Ebuenga

projects.title: Chat App
projects.summary: A real-time Chat App small project using React.js and PUSHER. It allows users to send and receive messages in real-time, with a simple and intuitive interface.
projects.overview: Real-time chat applications enable users to communicate instantly by sending and receiving messages, sharing files, and exchanging information efficiently, providing a seamless and interactive communication experience.
features: Moment-based navigation with a single 'cash pulse' at the top of every screen
Plain-language transaction summaries written as sentences, not line items
Haptic-first alerts that only interrupt for what genuinely matters
A tax-season mode that pre-assembles categories for bookkeeping

projects.title: Wavelength
projects.summary: A quieter alternative to the feed — audio conversations that people actually finish.
projects.overview: Wavelength is a social audio network built for people exhausted by algorithmic feeds. It organises conversation around places and moods rather than followers, and asks almost nothing of you to begin.
projects.challenge: Social apps optimise for time spent; listeners wanted time well spent. Retention data showed people loved content and hated the feed — endless, anxious, un-archivable.
projects.approach: We prototyped three navigation metaphors — map, timeline, and 'room'. Audio sketching with 60 participants steered us to a map of ongoing conversations. Design kept every interaction on a single thumb and gave hosts gentle structural tools to keep rooms calm.
projects.outcome: Median listening session grew from 9 to 23 minutes, while average time on feed fell sharply — people came for the signal and stayed for the conversation.
features: A map of live conversations, arranged by place and mood
Asynchronous voice notes that don't demand an audience
Room hosts get a 'quiet state' — an invite-only mode with barriers to entry
Auto-archiving with searchable transcripts and summaries

projects.title: Common Room
projects.summary: Booking and wayfinding for a national network of member workspaces — one legible system, forty rooms.
projects.overview: Common Room operates forty member workspaces across three cities. Their members booked desks and rooms through a patchwork of emails, spreadsheets, and sticky notes. We designed the single nervous system that replaced all three.
projects.challenge: Each workspace had its own quirks — a photograph studio that shouldn't be double-booked, a kitchen bench that only seated four. A one-size-fits-all booking tool would have failed within a week.
projects.approach: We built a configurable system: a typed 'space profile' per room, a wayfinding layer that mirrors the building, and a calendar that reads like a railway timetable. The whole thing degrades gracefully to a printed board for the rooms without screens.
projects.outcome: Double-bookings effectively eliminated, and the paperback 'room board' designs became so popular members asked for prints they could frame — which they did, 800 of them.
features: A per-space profile that encodes capacity, equipment, and house rules
Wayfinding that draws the actual floor plan, not a to-do list
A printed board export for rooms without displays
Fair-queue waitlists instead of instant-grab booking races

projects.title: Loom & Oak
projects.summary: A made-by-hand goods brand with a storefront that feels like walking into the workshop.
projects.overview: Loom & Oak makes wooden tools and objects in a single workshop in upstate New York. Their storefront had outgrown its off-the-shelf template long before the knurls and dovetails demanded better.
projects.challenge: A catalogue product photo page would have read every item as identical. Each object is different — a spoon and a mallet deserve different pacing, different stories, different amounts of white space.
projects.approach: We designed a 'living catalogue': products arranged editorially like an exhibition rather than a grid, with photography that changes the type treatment per material, and a checkout that quotes the maker's own words. Everything renders true-to-size against a measuring tape footer.
projects.outcome: Conversion up 41% holiday-over-holiday, average order value up 18%, and workshop visiting hours tripled — the storefront became a place people wanted to enter.
features: An editorial grid that matches pacing to object material and size
True-to-size photography with a working tape-measure motif
A checkout that reads like the maker's card, not a dunning letter
Maker-inventory: out-of-stock items become 'in the workshop'

projects.title: Signal
projects.summary: A sleep and recovery dashboard that tells one honest story per night — not a spreadsheet of guilt.
projects.overview: Signal connects to the sensors people already own and turns the noise into a single, legible read-out: how much recovery your body actually achieved today.
projects.challenge: Health data products have a shame problem. Users were abandoning dashboards full of red numbers and 'streaks' that punished rest. The honest metric — recovery — is the hardest to visualise well.
projects.approach: We treated the chart as the interface, not decoration: one main curve per day, a bespoke type scheme for the read-out, and a deliberate policy of never showing a trend line smaller than its own error. Morning checks became a ritual instead of an audit.
projects.outcome: Daily active use tripled, and the 'green day' ritual — a single confident metric you can plan around — became the product's signature screen.
features: One recovery read-out per day — a confidence interval, not a false precision
Morning ritual screen that takes ten seconds to answer
A guilt-free streak that counts rest, not consecutive logs
Dark mode tuned for a bedside glance at 6am

projects.title: Fieldnotes
projects.summary: A note-taking tool for researchers that makes messy fieldwork legible — without making it tidy.
projects.overview: Fieldnotes is where I quietly put my hardest constraint into practice: tools for people who live out of notebooks. It imports photos, scribbles, and audio, and turns a season of fieldwork into something you can cite.
projects.challenge: Researchers don't want a note app that imposes structure — imposing structure is the researcher's job. But a tool that stays formless can't be searched, linked, or finally written into a paper.
projects.approach: We studied how ten anthropologists actually wrote, then built an import pipeline that treats every kind of artifact the same: a dated note with provenance. Structure is a view, not a rule — you can read the same week as a timeline, a map, or a wall.
projects.outcome: Adopted by three university research groups in the first quarter, with a citation exporter that made it into the day-one of any grant application. It remains my favourite proof that constraint and freedom can share a tool.
features: One import pipeline for photos, scans, scribbles, and audio
Provenance baked in — every note remembers where it came from
Structure as a view: timeline, map, or 'the wall'
A citation exporter that understands academic practices
